title: Concentrate the promise on the force that moves desire.
dek: In Part II, Chapter 12 of Breakthrough Advertising, Eugene Schwartz shows how concentration gives a promise force by organizing attention around the single emotional drive most capable of producing action.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: A promise becomes easier to act on when its language gathers around one dominant force. Find the desire doing the real work, then remove the claims that compete with it.

canon.heading: Give the promise one emotional center.
canon.standfirst: Read the opening section of Part II, Chapter 12, "The Sixth Technique of Breakthrough Copy: Concentration," from Eugene Schwartz's Breakthrough Advertising on PDF pages 181-190. Schwartz shows how a message gains force when it concentrates attention on the dominant desire that can organize the prospect's action.
canon.readerIntro: Read this as a study of disciplined emphasis. Mark where Schwartz identifies the desire beneath the surface claim, gathers multiple details around one emotional force, or shows how competing appeals dilute response. Then write one concentrated-promise brief. Stop at PDF page 190.

blocks.label: 01 / Find the desire doing the work
paragraphs: A market may contain many wants, but a message becomes forceful when it discovers the desire most capable of organizing attention and action.
Read for the distinction between listing benefits and locating the emotional center that makes those benefits matter.

blocks.label: 02 / Concentration is selective emphasis
paragraphs: Concentration does not mean saying less by accident. It means selecting the promise, image, or consequence that can carry the rest of the argument.
Notice what happens when supporting details reinforce one dominant force instead of asking the prospect to process several unrelated appeals.

blocks.label: 03 / Let the market's desire set the direction
paragraphs: The copywriter's task is to enter the prospect's existing desire and give it a clearer path toward the offer.
Study how the message follows the force already present in the market rather than substituting the writer's preferred story.

blocks.label: 04 / Remove competing appeals
paragraphs: A message can become weaker by adding true but secondary benefits that pull attention away from the main reason to act.
Test each claim against the dominant desire: does it intensify the central promise, or does it create another center?

blocks.label: 05 / Write one concentrated-promise brief
paragraphs: Choose one offer and name its dominant customer desire, the single promise that speaks to it, and the supporting proof that strengthens that promise.
Stop with one concentrated-promise brief. Cut any detail that does not help the reader feel the central desire more clearly or believe the offer can answer it.

passageAnchors: the sixth technique of breakthrough copy
closeReading: Where does Schwartz distinguish a list of benefits from a concentrated appeal built around one dominant desire?
Which emotional force appears capable of organizing the prospect's attention and action, and what makes it dominant?
How do supporting details strengthen the central promise without becoming competing appeals?
Choose one offer. What is the customer's dominant desire, and what single promise speaks most directly to it?
Write one concentrated-promise brief with the dominant desire, the promise, and one proof point that reinforces it.

principle.heading: Make one desire impossible to miss.
principle.body: A persuasive message gains force when its claims, images, and proof gather around the dominant desire already moving the prospect. Concentration turns a crowded list of benefits into one memorable reason to act.
principle.example: A meal-planning service might offer convenience, savings, nutrition, and variety, but concentrate its opening promise on the exhausted parent who needs dinner solved by 6 p.m. The other benefits support that central relief instead of competing with it.
principle.practice: Choose one offer and write its dominant customer desire, one concentrated promise, and one proof point. Delete every benefit that does not intensify that promise.

output.heading: Concentrate before you amplify.
output.body: Find the desire with the greatest organizing power, make it the center of the promise, and let every supporting detail increase its force.

fieldNotes.title: Android is making scam protection part of the product promise
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Google announced new Android protections across calls, texts, and chat apps, including AI-assisted defenses against spoofed numbers, fake bank alerts, and AI voice-cloning scams.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: The dominant consumer desire is not abstract security; it is confidence that an ordinary message or call will not become an expensive mistake. The strongest product story concentrates the capability on that felt relief.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether scam prevention becomes a visible, everyday promise that earns trust before a user has to understand the underlying model or detection system.

fieldNotes.title: Meta lets people state the interest behind the feed
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Meta introduced AI-powered tools that let people shape what they see in Facebook Feed and Reels by describing their interests in their own words.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Personalization is being reframed from a hidden ranking mechanism into an explicit feeling of control. The promise is not merely more relevant content; it is a feed that better reflects the person using it.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether user-authored preference becomes a durable trust signal, or whether people still experience personalization as an opaque system making choices for them.

fieldNotes.title: Gen Alpha is a present influence, not only a future market
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Advertising Week marketers described Gen Alpha as influencing household purchases today, while also resisting the label of an AI generation and responding to creators, communities, and co-viewing experiences.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A broad demographic label hides several competing desires: influence, individuality, belonging, and discovery. The sharper brief starts with the human identity or community the brand can serve instead of leading with age or technology.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch for brands that use specific interests and creator communities as the organizing promise, rather than treating AI fluency as the audience's entire identity.

fieldNotes.title: Retail outlook improves, but the customer splits by ability to pay
fieldNotes.whatHappened: Moody's upgraded its global retail and apparel outlook to stable, while warning that consumption is increasingly bifurcated: upper-income households drive growth as lower- and middle-income shoppers focus on value and essentials.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A broad promise of growth hides two different customer desires. The sharper commercial message may be resilience and confidence for one segment, or dependable value and essentials for another.
fieldNotes.watch: Watch whether retailers split their proposition and proof by economic reality instead of using one optimistic message for customers experiencing very different pressures.

tweets.author: Ram Ahluwalia CFA, Lumida
tweets.title: A product fragment on turning capability into behavior
tweets.summary: This fragment is useful because it names the behavioral question behind a new capability. The important test is not whether the feature is impressive, but whether it changes a repeated workflow enough for the user to adopt it.
tweets.text:
THE EVENT HORIZON

We are in the fast take off world of AI.

Back in 2024, my view (below) was that we are in a ‘slow take off’ AI world we would see ‘AI microservices’.

Those AI microservices are called Agents.

And, the Agents on the high end models are better than humans.

The Agents interact and coordinate on complex objectives.

For the last 30 to 60 days, I am having a ‘wow’ moment with the frontier models thru our use and application nearly every day since Astra and Opus 5.5.

I am not referring merely to delegated work or creating decks, etc.

That was six to nine months ago - a pure productivity story… not a labor substitution story.

The slow take off world gives us all time to adapt new norms and patterns.

The Fast Takeoff AI world creates social anxiety.

It also does not give time to adapt.

Either you disrupt yourself and your workflows or you get disrupted.

Where we are now reminds me of a scene in a movie where you are watching the tidal wave roll in from the beach….

It’s also accelerating in part because engineers are not a constraint.

Vision and initiative are all you need now.

I do think a number of white collar services industries are going to be swallowed whole.

Humans will hold licenses but AIs will do the driving.

Here’s the funny dynamic.

We are on the exponential now.

Ask yourself what your team was doing 1 year ago.

The opportunity cost of time now is very high.

Each day you don’t build a workflow you are not compounding.

The productivity rate that is coming means that you need to use AI - every day and every person in your org - or you will be trampled by others using AI.

Here’s a north star:

Every single department / function you have needs a Meta Agent executive.

*Your staff meeting should round robin with Meta Agents.*

If you are not architecting your enterprise with that north star you are not riding the wave.

The Meta Agent has agendas, joins zoom calls, leads directs and coaches.

Stop thinking of AI as ‘doing work’ and start thinking about AI leadership (eg, governing work).

That last step - AI leadership, not AI grunt work - could take another year to crack if you’re running fast.

Maybe 6 months.

If you get there, you win all the marbles.
